criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking and domestic water service access, specifically Level III piped water connections from the Leyte Metropolitan Water District (LMWD)/PrimeWater as well as reliance on Level I/II communal faucets, deep wells, tank deliveries, and informal water peddlers in four permanent post-Typhoon Haiyan resettlement villages.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study analyses multiple legal, administrative, institutional, and governance drivers of post-disaster resettlement water services (the No Build Zone relocation policy, interagency coordination and LWUA/LMWD procurement delays, and regime shifts in housing construction). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, the paper also directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) utility ownership and statutory/regulatory governance structure directly governing service access—specifically Presidential Decree No. 198's 75% active-connection threshold vs. Supreme Court ruling G.R. No. 197146's 50%+1 connection rule for Highly Urbanized Cities determining LMWD Board appointment authority (which shaped bulk vs. individual household metering practices, deterred pipe expansion into Tacloban North, and triggered a 2018-2019 dual-board standoff disrupting billing/services and delaying resettlement connections), alongside the 2019 Public-Private Partnership Joint Venture Agreement (JVA) semi-privatizing operations under PrimeWater while LMWD retained regulatory control; (2) regulatory/technical compliance rules, where housing subcontractors installed pipes non-compliant with water district specifications and disregarded building/development permits, halting connection of subdivision distribution pipes to LMWD mainlines; and (3) water connection application burdens and monthly tariff/bill unaffordability driving low (35%) Level III connection uptake and rapid post-connection attrition.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical mixed-methods study conducted from June 2022 to March 2023 combining a quota-sampled household survey (n = 400; 100 per resettlement village), focus group discussions (8 participants per FGD), 51 semi-structured key informant interviews, community walkthroughs, and content analysis of government/audit reports.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household water service outcomes including perceived availability of drinking water (74%) and general household water (70%) across 400 surveyed households, village-level Level III piped connection status (none, partial, or intermittent) and Tacloban North Level III uptake (35% as of March 2022), reliance on wells/communal taps/peddlers, unit prices paid to peddlers (PHP 30 per jug for drinking water; PHP 10 per jug for general use), and non-uptake or loss of piped connection due to monthly bill unaffordability.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and units of analysis (Typhoon Haiyan-displaced households in four resettlement villages in Tacloban City and Palo, Leyte, n = 400 surveyed households, FGDs, and 51 key informants; household, resettlement subdivision, and water utility/governance levels), legal/institutional exposures, water access/affordability outcomes, and mixed-methods case study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English (with fieldwork instruments translated into Waray-Waray for data collection).

raw_response.exposure: Water governance and regulatory mechanisms affecting post-Haiyan resettlement villages: statutory/judicial water district board-appointment connection-share rules (PD No. 198 75% rule and Supreme Court G.R. No. 197146 50%+1 rule), utility semi-privatization via the 2019 LMWD-PrimeWater PPP Joint Venture Agreement, non-compliance with water district pipe specifications and building/development permits, centralized vs. local procurement/bidding rules, No Build Zone relocation policy, and monthly water bill costs.
raw_response.outcome: Household piped water connection status and uptake (Level III connectivity at 35% in Tacloban North; zero or partial block-level connections across the four study villages), perceived drinking (74%) and general-use (70%) water availability, supply intermittency, reliance on communal faucets/deep wells/water peddlers, and affordability-driven non-connection or disconnection after a few months.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Typhoon Haiyan-displaced households residing in four permanent resettlement subdivisions in Tacloban City (DREAMVille, Villa Sofia) and Palo, Leyte (Habitat for Humanity, Ver Dominic Heights), Philippines: quota-sampled survey of 400 households (100 per site), focus group discussions (8 participants each), and 51 semi-structured key informant interviews with homeowners' associations, LGUs, water utility, and national agency officials.
raw_response.rationale: This mixed-methods empirical study in four post-Haiyan resettlement villages in the Philippines meets all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). Beyond broader post-disaster project delivery and relocation planning, it empirically examines specific rule-type legal, regulatory, and utility-ownership mechanisms directly governing household water service access—including PD No. 198 and Supreme Court G.R. No. 197146 active-connection threshold rules governing LMWD Board control (linked to bulk metering, restricted network expansion, and a two-year governance standoff), semi-privatization under the 2019 LMWD-PrimeWater PPP Joint Venture Agreement, contractor non-compliance with water district pipe specifications blocking mainline connection, and monthly water bill unaffordability limiting Level III connection uptake and retention.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods empirical case study (cross-sectional quota-sampled household survey n=400 with descriptive statistics, focus group discussions, 51 key informant interviews, community walkthroughs, and document analysis)
